segment: The conversation drew Mara’s attention in. She almost forgot how much she was focusing on their movements, and how many ways they were expressing themselves through nonverbal cues. The brown-haired newcomer, still carrying that same plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo and the red liquid in it, was now explaining about a recent project when he spotted Mara, took two steps toward her, and paused a little way off to shake hands and exchange names. She reached out for his hand, but when he didn’t take hers he dropped down into the low seat instead, letting their fingertips touch just before the handshake was supposed to happen, and he leaned in closer than she expected; she straightened a bit more formally, trying to remind herself that they weren’t yet friends.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

segment:
As he set down the glass and moved out of its space, a previously unseen catering worker entered from the hallway behind him and retrieved it. She wore the same black-and-white striped Fulcrum uniform shirt, though she looked old enough to have had that job since the Institute was founded; and she gave no outward sign of the social fact that she was taking their discarded drink back to the kitchen, while the rest of the conversation went on.

Mara watched this woman return to the hallway where she belonged, and noticed herself noticing who assumed whose labor.

segment:
By six forty-five there were eight men, four women, and two children in the common room at Fulcrum. Two more women in white lab coats with “FULCRUM” stitched above the pockets pushed open a pair of glass doors down the hallway, announcing themselves to the group, and Mara recognized one as Dr. Grace Williams, Jonah Reed’s boss.

In the last half-hour, Mara had watched the young fellow who first introduced himself to her take a glass of white wine from the bar across the room and bring it back to join the crowd standing against the wall on the left side of the door. When she followed his eyes over to see who he’d been looking at, she noticed an older catering worker had taken hold of his abandoned glass, lifted it up from the table where he’d set it down, and turned on a heel to walk right out.

segment:
But as soon as Jonah and the brown-haired man started talking, another man emerged from the hallway into the main room: an older man. He was tall enough to be conspicuous at that point of the conversation, and he had dark hair slicked back from a ruddy face. A name tag said Jonah Reed.

Mara waited for the old man to introduce himself as Jonah, but he didn’t say a word as he walked past them toward the far door, leaving Mara unsure of how to respond—should she have expected him to stop and talk with them? But since he was carrying a clear glass bottle from which he drank continuously, she guessed that he must have been just leaving the kitchen and making his way home.

And sure enough, the door at the other end swung shut behind him, and then nothing more happened for about a minute.

segment:
Once all three of them were settled around the low table, the brown-haired man raised his glass again and took another sip before setting it back down between Jonah’s crossed ankles and glancing at Mara. “I haven’t had a chance to meet you yet. I’m Tim. We’re in the same cohort.”
Mara nodded hello, and then noticed that one of the catering staff had picked up Tim’s glass and set it aside without remark. Jonah’s knees parted, releasing the plastic cup onto the carpet.

The brown-haired man took no notice, just carried on his casual conversation while a woman walked over from across the room with his empty glass in one hand. She was taller, heavier, older; her short brown hair was streaked with gray and she had the look of a woman who has spent a lifetime managing people.
The older catering worker placed his empty cup on the edge of the table without so much as a glance at him. And when she turned and walked away, Tim didn’t even bother to follow with his eyes.
